claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins in a high-temperature, single-phase BCC state.
Severe plastic deformation introduces a high dislocation density in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Severe plastic deformation refines the grains and increases grain-boundary density in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
SPD-generated dislocations and grain boundaries act as fast diffusion pathways during annealing.
Defect-assisted diffusion creates localized compositional inhomogeneities in the alloy.
Localized compositional inhomogeneities serve as nucleation sites for secondary phases.
SPD-induced defects lower local diffusion barriers during annealing.
Segregation shifts local compositions into regimes where secondary phases are thermodynamically favored over homogeneous BCC.
SPD followed by step-wise annealing drives decomposition of BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The decomposition may produce two distinct BCC variants with different lattice parameters.
The decomposition may produce an HCP secondary phase at sufficiently high strain and annealing temperature.
The decomposition may produce an FCC secondary phase in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The secondary phases induced by SPD and annealing would not form under conventional cooling without SPD.
Phase decomposition should be pronounced only when substantial defect density is retained while annealing provides atomic mobility without complete homogenization.
Insufficient strain or annealing conditions that prevent segregation should markedly reduce or eliminate phase decomposition.
Relative to the non-SPD baseline, the SPD-annealed alloy should show split BCC peaks or additional phase peaks in XRD or TEM.
SPD-induced phase decomposition should change hardness or ductility relative to the baseline.
In HfNbTiZr, annealing after HPT decomposed a single BCC phase into two BCC phases at 740 K, produced HCP at high strain above 890 K, and was accompanied by chemical heterogeneity.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is stated to apply only when SPD creates and preserves a significantly different defect structure, but the falsification rule requires observing no significant difference in defect structure between SPD and control samples. That result would indicate failure to meet the hypothesis's applicability condition rather than decisively falsifying defect-driven segregation.
